title: Part 5, Chapter 3
paragraphs: "Pyotr Petrovitch," she cried, "protect me... you at least! Make this foolish woman understand she can't treat a lady in misfortune like this... There are laws against such things... I'll go to the governor-general himself... She will answer for this... Remembering my father's hospitality, protect these orphans."

"Allow me, madam... allow me." Pyotr Petrovitch waved her off. "As you are well aware, I did not have the honor of knowing your papa" (someone laughed out loud) "and I have no intention of getting involved in your endless squabbles with Amalia Ivanovna... I've come here on my own business... and I need to speak with your stepdaughter, Sofya... Ivanovna, I believe? Let me through."
Pyotr Petrovitch edged past her and went to the opposite corner where Sonia was standing.

Katerina Ivanovna stood frozen in place, as if struck by lightning. She couldn't understand how Pyotr Petrovitch could deny having enjoyed her father's hospitality. Though she'd invented the whole thing herself, she had come to believe it completely. She was also struck by Pyotr Petrovitch's businesslike, dry, and even contemptuous tone. The noise gradually died down as he entered. Not only was this "serious businessman" strikingly out of place at the gathering, but it was clear he had come on some important matter, that something exceptional must have brought him, and that something was about to happen. Raskolnikov, standing beside Sonia, stepped aside to let him pass; Pyotr Petrovitch didn't seem to notice him. A minute later Lebeziatnikov also appeared in the doorway; he didn't come in but stood listening with obvious interest, almost wonder, and seemed confused for a time.

"Forgive me for possibly interrupting, but it's a matter of some importance," Pyotr Petrovitch observed, addressing the company in general. "I'm glad to find other people present. Amalia Ivanovna, I humbly ask you, as mistress of the house, to pay careful attention to what I have to say to Sofya Ivanovna. Sofya Ivanovna," he continued, turning to Sonia, who was very surprised and already alarmed, "immediately after your visit, I found that a hundred-ruble note was missing from my table, in the room of my friend Mr. Lebeziatnikov. If you know in any way where it is now and will tell us, I give you my word of honor, with all present as witnesses, that the matter will end there. Otherwise, I will be forced to take very serious measures, and then... you'll have only yourself to blame."
Complete silence fell over the room. Even the crying children went quiet. Sonia stood deathly pale, staring at Luzhin, unable to say a word. She seemed not to understand. Several seconds passed.
"Well, what's it to be then?" asked Luzhin, looking at her intently.
"I don't know... I know nothing about it," Sonia said faintly at last.

"No, you know nothing?" Luzhin repeated, and paused again for a few seconds. "Think carefully, mademoiselle," he began severely, though still with a tone of admonishment. "Consider. I'm willing to give you time to think it over. Please understand: if I were not absolutely certain, I would never, with my experience, risk accusing you so directly. For such a direct accusation before witnesses, if it turned out to be false or even mistaken, I would bear some responsibility myself. I'm aware of that. This morning I cashed several five-percent bonds for approximately three thousand rubles. The figures are noted in my pocketbook. When I got home, I counted the money — as Mr. Lebeziatnikov will confirm — and after counting two thousand three hundred rubles, I put the rest in my pocketbook in my coat pocket. About five hundred rubles remained on the table, including three hundred-ruble notes. At that moment you came in, at my invitation, and the entire time you were here, you were extremely agitated — three times you jumped up in the middle of our conversation and tried to leave. Mr. Lebeziatnikov can confirm this. You yourself, mademoiselle, will probably not deny that I invited you through Mr. Lebeziatnikov solely to discuss the hopeless and destitute situation of your relative, Katerina Ivanovna, whose dinner I was unable to attend, and the possibility of organizing some kind of subscription or lottery for her benefit. You thanked me and even shed tears. I describe all this exactly as it happened, first to remind you, and second to show that not the slightest detail has escaped my memory. Then I took a ten-ruble note from the table and gave it to you as my initial contribution for your relative's benefit. Mr. Lebeziatnikov saw all of this. Then I walked you to the door — you were still in the same agitated state — after which, left alone with Mr. Lebeziatnikov, I spoke with him for about ten minutes. Then Mr. Lebeziatnikov went out and I returned to the table where the money lay, intending to count it and set it aside as I had planned. To my surprise, one hundred-ruble note had disappeared. Consider the situation carefully. I cannot suspect Mr. Lebeziatnikov — the very idea is beneath me. I cannot have miscounted, because just before you arrived I had finished my accounts and found the total correct. You'll admit that, given your agitation, your eagerness to leave, the fact that your hands were on the table for some time, and considering your social position and the habits associated with it, I was — so to speak, with horror and very much against my will — compelled to form a suspicion: a cruel but justified suspicion! I'll add further that despite my firm conviction, I realize I'm taking a certain risk in making this accusation. But as you can see, I could not let it go. I have taken action, and I'll tell you why: solely, madam, solely because of your black ingratitude! I invite you to help your destitute relative, I give you my donation of ten rubles, and you immediately repay me with such an act. It's outrageous! You need a lesson. Think it over! As a true friend — and you could have no better friend right now — I urge you to consider what you're doing, or I will not relent! Well, what do you say?"
"I took nothing," Sonia whispered in terror. "You gave me ten rubles — here, take it back."
Sonia pulled a handkerchief from her pocket, untied a corner of it, took out the ten-ruble note, and held it out to Luzhin.
"And the hundred rubles — you won't admit to taking those?" he pressed reproachfully, not taking the note.

Sonia looked around. Everyone was staring at her with terrible, stern, mocking, hostile eyes. She looked at Raskolnikov... He stood against the wall with his arms crossed, looking at her with burning eyes.
"Good God!" escaped from Sonia.
"Amalia Ivanovna, we'll need to notify the police, so I humbly ask you to send for the building superintendent in the meantime," Luzhin said softly and almost kindly.
"Gott der Barmherzige! I knew she was the thief!" cried Amalia Ivanovna, throwing up her hands.
"You knew it?" Luzhin seized on this. "Then I take it you had some prior reason for thinking so. I ask you, worthy Amalia Ivanovna, to remember what you just said — you've spoken before witnesses."
A buzz of loud conversation erupted from all sides. Everyone was stirring.
"What!" cried Katerina Ivanovna, suddenly grasping the situation, and she rushed at Luzhin. "What! You're accusing her of stealing? Sonia? You wretches, you wretches!"
She ran to Sonia, threw her wasted arms around her, and held her tight as a vise.
"Sonia! How dare you take ten rubles from him? Foolish girl! Give it to me! Give me the ten rubles right now — here!"

Snatching the note from Sonia, Katerina Ivanovna crumpled it up and flung it straight into Luzhin's face. It hit him in the eye and fell to the floor. Amalia Ivanovna scrambled to pick it up. Pyotr Petrovitch lost his temper.
"Restrain that mad woman!" he shouted.
At that moment several other people appeared in the doorway alongside Lebeziatnikov, including two ladies.

"What! Mad? Am I mad? Idiot!" shrieked Katerina Ivanovna. "You're the idiot, you petty lawyer, you vile man! Sonia, Sonia, take his money! Sonia, a thief! She'd give away her last kopeck!" Katerina Ivanovna broke into hysterical laughter. "Have you ever seen such an idiot?" She turned from side to side. "And you too?" She suddenly spotted the landlady. "You too, sausage-eater! You're calling her a thief, you trashy Prussian hen-leg in a crinoline! She hasn't been out of this room — she came straight from your place and sat down beside me. Everyone saw it. She was sitting right here, next to Rodion Romanovitch. Search her! Since she hasn't left the room, the money would have to be on her! Go ahead, search her! But if you don't find it, then excuse me, my dear fellow, you'll answer for it! I'll go to our Sovereign, to our gracious Tsar himself, and throw myself at his feet — today, this very minute! I'm alone in the world! They'd let me in! You think they wouldn't? You're wrong — I will get in! You counted on her meekness! You relied on that! But I'm not so submissive, let me tell you! You've gone too far. Search her, search her!"
Katerina Ivanovna, frenzied, shook Luzhin and dragged him toward Sonia.

"I'm ready, I'll take responsibility... but please calm down, madam, calm down. I see you're not so submissive after all!... Well, well, but as for the search..." Luzhin stammered, "that should really be done before the police... though there are enough witnesses as it is... I'm willing... But it's rather awkward for a man... given her sex... But with Amalia Ivanovna's help... though of course that's not the proper way to do things... How should we proceed?"

"Anyone who wants can search her!" cried Katerina Ivanovna. "Sonia, turn out your pockets! See! Look, you monster — the pocket's empty! Here was her handkerchief! Here's the other pocket — look! See, you see?"

Katerina Ivanovna turned — or rather yanked — both pockets inside out. But from the right pocket a piece of paper flew out, traced a curve through the air, and landed at Luzhin's feet. Everyone saw it; several cried out. Pyotr Petrovitch bent down, picked up the paper between two fingers, held it up where everyone could see it, and unfolded it. It was a hundred-ruble note folded into eighths. Pyotr Petrovitch displayed it for all to see.
"Thief! Out of my apartment! Police, police!" yelled Amalia Ivanovna. "They must be sent to Siberia! Get out!"

Exclamations rose from all sides. Raskolnikov stayed silent, keeping his eyes fixed on Sonia, with only an occasional quick glance at Luzhin. Sonia stood motionless, as if unconscious. She could barely feel surprise. Suddenly color rushed to her cheeks; she cried out and hid her face in her hands.
"No, it wasn't me! I didn't take it! I know nothing about it!" she cried with a heartrending wail, rushing to Katerina Ivanovna, who clasped her tightly, as though to shield her from the whole world.

"Sonia! Sonia! I don't believe it! You see — I don't believe it!" she cried in the face of the obvious evidence, rocking her in her arms like a baby, kissing her face over and over, then grabbing her hands and kissing them too. "You took it! How stupid these people are! You fools, all of you!" she cried, addressing the entire room. "You don't know, you don't know what a heart she has, what kind of girl she is! Her, steal? She'd sell her last scrap of clothing, she'd go barefoot to help you if you needed it — that's who she is! She has the yellow card because my children were starving — she sold herself for us! Oh, husband, husband! Do you see? Do you see? What a memorial dinner for you! Merciful heavens! Defend her — why are you all just standing there? Rodion Romanovitch, why won't you stand up for her? Do you believe it too? None of you are worth her little finger! God, defend her now!"

The wailing of the poor, consumptive, helpless woman seemed to produce a powerful effect on her audience. The agonized, wasted, consumptive face, the cracked blood-stained lips, the hoarse voice, the tears flowing freely as a child's, the trusting, childlike yet despairing plea for help — it was all so pitiful that everyone seemed to feel for her. Pyotr Petrovitch was at least immediately moved to compassion.

"Madam, madam, this doesn't reflect on you at all!" he cried impressively. "No one would dream of accusing you of being involved or even of being an accomplice, especially since you proved her guilt yourself by turning out her pockets, showing you had no prior knowledge. I'm perfectly ready, perfectly ready to show compassion if poverty, so to speak, drove Sofya Semyonovna to it. But why did you refuse to confess, mademoiselle? Were you afraid of the disgrace? Your first time? You lost your composure, perhaps? Quite understandable... But how could you sink to such an act? Gentlemen," he addressed the whole room, "gentlemen! Feeling compassion for these people, I'm ready to forgive it all even now, despite the personal insult I've received. And may this disgrace serve as a lesson to you in future," he said to Sonia. "I'll take the matter no further. Enough!"

Pyotr Petrovitch stole a glance at Raskolnikov. Their eyes met, and the fire in Raskolnikov's seemed ready to burn him to ashes. Meanwhile, Katerina Ivanovna appeared to hear nothing. She was kissing and hugging Sonia like a madwoman. The children were also pressing around Sonia from all sides, and Polenka — though she didn't fully understand what was happening — was drowning in tears and shaking with sobs, burying her pretty little face, swollen from crying, against Sonia's shoulder.
"How despicable!" a loud voice suddenly rang out from the doorway.
Pyotr Petrovitch spun around quickly.
"What vileness!" Lebeziatnikov repeated, staring him straight in the face.
Pyotr Petrovitch actually flinched — everyone noticed and remembered it later. Lebeziatnikov strode into the room.
"And you dared to call me as a witness?" he said, walking right up to Pyotr Petrovitch.
"What do you mean? What are you talking about?" Luzhin muttered.
"I mean that you... are a slanderer — that's what my words mean!" Lebeziatnikov said hotly, fixing him with a stern look through his nearsighted eyes.
He was extremely angry. Raskolnikov watched him intently, as though weighing every word. Again there was silence. Pyotr Petrovitch seemed almost struck dumb, at least for the first moment.
"If that's directed at me..." he began, stammering. "But what's wrong with you? Have you lost your mind?"

"I'm perfectly sane, but you're a scoundrel! How despicable! I heard everything. I waited on purpose to make sure I understood, because I'll admit even now the logic isn't entirely clear to me... What you did it all for, I can't grasp."
"What exactly have I done? Stop talking in your ridiculous riddles! Or are you drunk?"

"You might be the drunkard, you vile man, but I'm not! I never touch vodka — it's against my principles. Listen to this, everyone: he himself, with his own hands, gave Sofya Semyonovna that hundred-ruble note! I saw it — I'm a witness, and I'll swear to it! He did it, he did it!" Lebeziatnikov repeated, addressing the whole room.
"Are you out of your mind, you fool?" squealed Luzhin. "She herself just told everyone, right in front of you, that I only gave her ten rubles. How could I have given it to her?"

"I saw it! I saw it!" Lebeziatnikov insisted. "And even though it's against my principles, I'm ready this very minute to swear any oath you want in court, because I saw you slip it into her pocket. Only I was fool enough to think you did it out of kindness! When you were saying goodbye at the door, while you held her hand in one hand, you slipped the note into her pocket with the other — the left one. I saw it!"
Luzhin turned pale.
"What lies!" he cried brazenly. "How could you, standing by the window, have seen the note? You imagined it with your nearsighted eyes. You're raving!"

"No, I didn't imagine it. And even though I was standing some distance away, I saw everything clearly. True, it would have been hard to identify a banknote from the window — you're right about that — but I happened to know it was a hundred-ruble note, because when you were about to give Sofya Semyonovna ten rubles, you picked up a hundred-ruble note from the table. I saw it because I was standing close by at that moment, and an idea immediately struck me, so I didn't forget you had it in your hand. You folded it and kept holding it. I didn't think about it again until you were getting up, when you shifted it from your right hand to your left and nearly dropped it. I noticed because the same idea occurred to me again — that you meant to do her a secret kindness without me seeing. You can imagine how closely I was watching after that, and I saw you succeed in slipping it into her pocket. I saw it! I'll take an oath on it!"

Lebeziatnikov was almost out of breath. Exclamations rose from all sides, mostly expressing astonishment, but some sounding menacing. Everyone crowded around Pyotr Petrovitch. Katerina Ivanovna rushed to Lebeziatnikov.
"I was wrong about you! Protect her! You're the only one defending her! She's an orphan — God has sent you!"
Katerina Ivanovna, barely knowing what she was doing, sank to her knees before him.

"Utter nonsense!" Luzhin roared, furious. "Everything you've said is nonsense! 'An idea struck you, you didn't think, you noticed' — what does any of it prove? So I slipped it to her secretly, on purpose? What for? What reason? What do I have to do with this...?"

"What for? That's what I can't figure out either, but what I'm telling you is a fact — I'm certain of it! Far from being mistaken, you despicable criminal, I remember that a question occurred to me right then, just as I was thanking you and shaking your hand. Why did you put it in her pocket secretly? Why the secrecy? Was it just to hide it from me, knowing my principles oppose private charity as it doesn't achieve any fundamental cure? Well, I decided you must have been ashamed to give such a large sum in front of me. Then I thought maybe you wanted to surprise her — when she'd find a whole hundred-ruble note in her pocket. I know some charitable people love staging their good deeds that way. Then another idea struck me: you wanted to test her, to see if she'd come to thank you when she found it. Then I thought you just wanted to avoid being thanked — as the saying goes, your right hand shouldn't know what your left hand does. I considered so many possibilities that I put off examining it further, though I did feel it would be tactless to show you I knew your secret. But then yet another thought struck me: that Sofya Semyonovna might easily lose the money before she noticed it. That's why I decided to come find her, to tell her you'd put a hundred rubles in her pocket. But on the way I stopped at Madame Kobilatnikov's to drop off the 'General Treatise on the Positive Method,' especially recommending Piderit's article and Wagner's. Then I come here and find — this! Now, could I have had all these thoughts and considerations if I hadn't actually seen you put the hundred-ruble note in her pocket?"

By the time Lebeziatnikov finished his long-winded speech, complete with its logical conclusion, he was quite exhausted, and perspiration was streaming down his face. Unfortunately, he couldn't even express himself properly in Russian, though he knew no other language, so he was completely drained, almost gaunt after this heroic effort. But his speech produced a powerful effect. He'd spoken with such passion, such conviction, that everyone clearly believed him. Pyotr Petrovitch felt that things were going very badly for him.

"What do I care if stupid ideas popped into your head?" he shouted. "That's not evidence. You could have dreamed it all! I'm telling you, you're lying, sir! Lying and slandering me out of spite, simply because I refused to go along with your godless, free-thinking social ideas!"
But this retort did not help Pyotr Petrovitch. Murmurs of disapproval came from all sides.

"Oh, so that's your tack now, is it?" cried Lebeziatnikov. "That's absurd! Call the police — I'll take my oath! There's only one thing I can't understand: what made him risk such a contemptible act. What a pitiful, despicable man!"
"I can explain why he risked it, and if necessary, I'll swear to it too," Raskolnikov said at last in a firm voice, stepping forward.
He appeared calm and composed. Everyone felt clearly, just from looking at him, that he really did know the answer and that the mystery was about to be solved.

"Now I can explain it all," said Raskolnikov, addressing Lebeziatnikov. "From the very beginning, I suspected there was some vile scheme behind this. I began to suspect it based on certain circumstances known only to me, which I'll share with everyone now — they explain everything. Your valuable testimony has made it all clear. I ask everyone to listen. This man" — he pointed at Luzhin — "was recently engaged to my sister, Avdotya Romanovna Raskolnikov. But upon arriving in Petersburg, he quarreled with me at our first meeting the day before yesterday, and I threw him out of my room. I have two witnesses to that. He's a very spiteful man... The day before yesterday, I didn't know he was staying here in your room, and so on that very same day — the day we quarreled — he saw me give money to Katerina Ivanovna for the funeral, as a friend of the late Mr. Marmeladov. He immediately wrote to my mother claiming I'd given all my money not to Katerina Ivanovna but to Sofya Semyonovna, making the most contemptible insinuations about my relationship with Sofya Semyonovna. All this was designed to turn my mother and sister against me, by suggesting I was squandering on unworthy things the money they'd sent — their last money. Yesterday evening, in front of my mother, my sister, and Luzhin himself, I stated that I'd given the money to Katerina Ivanovna for the funeral, not to Sofya Semyonovna, and that I had no acquaintance with Sofya Semyonovna and had never even seen her before. I added that Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin, with all his fine qualities, wasn't worth Sofya Semyonovna's little finger, despite his speaking so badly of her. When he asked whether I'd seat Sofya Semyonovna next to my sister, I replied that I'd already done so that day. Outraged that my mother and sister refused to quarrel with me based on his insinuations, he grew inexcusably rude to them. A final break occurred and he was thrown out of the house. All of this happened yesterday evening. Now pay special attention to this: if he had succeeded today in proving Sofya Semyonovna was a thief, he would have shown my mother and sister that he was nearly right in his suspicions — that he'd had good reason to be angry at my putting my sister on a level with Sofya Semyonovna — that by attacking me, he'd been protecting my sister's honor. In short, through all this he might even have managed to set my family against me, and he no doubt hoped to be restored to their good graces — to say nothing of his personal revenge on me, since he has reason to believe that Sofya Semyonovna's honor and happiness matter greatly to me. That's what he was scheming. That's the whole explanation, and there can be no other!"

That was roughly how Raskolnikov concluded his speech, which was heard very attentively though frequently interrupted by exclamations from the audience. Despite the interruptions, he spoke clearly, calmly, precisely, and firmly. His decisive voice, his tone of conviction, and his stern expression made a powerful impression on everyone.

"Yes, yes, that's exactly it!" Lebeziatnikov confirmed enthusiastically. "It must be, because he asked me, as soon as Sofya Semyonovna came into our room, whether you were here — whether I'd seen you among Katerina Ivanovna's guests. He called me over to the window and asked me in secret. It was essential for him that you be here! That's it — that's exactly it!"

Luzhin smiled contemptuously and said nothing. But he was very pale. He seemed to be calculating some means of escape. Perhaps he would gladly have simply left, but at that point it was practically impossible — leaving would have been an admission that the accusations against him were true. Besides, the crowd, already worked up by drink, was now far too agitated to let him go. The commissariat clerk, who hadn't fully grasped the situation, was shouting louder than anyone and making suggestions highly unpleasant for Luzhin. But not everyone present was drunk — lodgers had come in from every room. The three Poles were tremendously excited, shouting at him constantly: "The pan is a scoundrel!" and muttering threats in Polish. Sonia had been listening with strained attention, though she too seemed unable to take it all in; she looked as if she were just coming to. She kept her eyes on Raskolnikov, sensing that all her safety lay with him. Katerina Ivanovna was breathing hard and painfully, looking terribly exhausted. Amalia Ivanovna stood there looking more bewildered than anyone, mouth hanging open, unable to make out what had happened. She only understood that Pyotr Petrovitch had somehow come to grief.

Raskolnikov tried to speak again, but they wouldn't let him. Everyone was crowding around Luzhin with threats and shouts of abuse. But Pyotr Petrovitch was not intimidated. Seeing that his accusation of Sonia had completely collapsed, he resorted to brazenness:

"Let me through, gentlemen, let me through! Don't crowd me!" he said, pushing through the mob. "And spare me the threats, please! I assure you they're useless. On the contrary, you'll be held responsible, gentlemen, for violently obstructing justice. The thief has been more than exposed, and I shall prosecute. Our judges are not so blind and... not so drunk, and will not take the word of two notorious troublemakers, atheists, and agitators accusing me out of personal vengeance — which they're foolish enough to admit... Yes, let me through!"

"I don't want to find a single trace of you in my room! Get out at once, and everything between us is finished! When I think of the trouble I've gone to, the way I've been lecturing you... this entire fortnight!"
"I told you myself today I was leaving, when you tried to keep me. I'll simply add that you're a fool. I suggest you see a doctor about your brains and your eyesight. Let me pass, gentlemen!"

He forced his way through. But the commissariat clerk wasn't prepared to let him off so easily: he grabbed a glass from the table, waved it in the air, and hurled it at Pyotr Petrovitch — but it flew straight into Amalia Ivanovna instead. She screamed, and the clerk, losing his balance, crashed heavily under the table. Pyotr Petrovitch made his way to his room and half an hour later had left the building. Sonia, timid by nature, had always known she was more vulnerable to mistreatment than anyone, that she could be wronged with impunity. Until that day she'd believed she might escape misfortune through care, gentleness, and meekness toward everyone. Her disappointment was too great. She could bear almost anything with patience and scarcely a complaint — even this. But in those first moments it was too bitter. Despite her vindication and her triumph — once the initial terror and shock had passed and she could see things clearly — the feeling of helplessness and of the wrong done to her filled her heart with anguish, and she was overcome by hysterical weeping. Finally, unable to endure any more, she rushed from the room and ran home, almost immediately after Luzhin's departure. When the glass flew at Amalia Ivanovna amid loud laughter, it was more than the landlady could stand. She let out a shriek and flew at Katerina Ivanovna like a fury, blaming her for everything.
"Out of my apartment! This instant! Get out!"

She began snatching up everything she could lay hands on that belonged to Katerina Ivanovna and hurling it to the floor. Katerina Ivanovna, pale, almost fainting, gasping for breath, sprang from the bed where she'd collapsed in exhaustion and rushed at Amalia Ivanovna. But the battle was hopelessly one-sided: the landlady swatted her away like a feather.

"What! As if that godless slander weren't enough — this vile creature attacks me! On the day of my husband's funeral, I'm thrown out of my home! After eating my bread and salt, she throws me into the street with my orphans! Where am I supposed to go?" wailed the poor woman, sobbing and gasping. "God!" she cried, her eyes flashing. "Is there no justice on earth? Who should You protect if not us orphans? We'll see! There is law and justice on this earth — there is, and I'll find it! Just wait, you godless creature! Polenka, stay with the children — I'll be back. Wait for me, even if you have to wait in the street. We'll see whether there's any justice left!"

Throwing that green shawl over her head — the one Marmeladov had mentioned to Raskolnikov — Katerina Ivanovna squeezed through the rowdy, drunken crowd of lodgers still filling the room and ran out into the street, wailing and weeping, with some vague intention of immediately going to find justice. Polenka, clutching the two little ones in her arms, crouched terrified on the trunk in the corner, waiting trembling for her mother's return. Amalia Ivanovna stormed around the room, shrieking, wailing, and hurling everything she came across to the floor. The lodgers talked all at once — some commenting on what had happened, others quarreling and swearing, still others breaking into song...
"Now it's time for me to go," Raskolnikov thought. "Well, Sofya Semyonovna, we'll see what you have to say now!"
And he set off toward Sonia's lodgings.
